agent: A single illustration depicts a split scene: on the left, a user sits at a laptop with the lid closed, handing a written task card to a central humanoid robot labeled “Lead Agent (Chief of Staff),” who stands at a large desk; from this robot’s back and shoulders extend multiple articulated arms, each reaching to a different floating icon—a web browser window, a code editor with lines of text, a magnifying glass over a search bar, a gear-shaped software control panel, and two smaller robot figures labeled “Sub-agents.” The desk also holds a clock face and a progress bar partially filled, indicating work continuing over time. benchmark: The illustration shows a large, multi-panel scoreboard at the center of a bright testing hall, where several stylized AI models—each drawn as a distinct robot with a nameplate like “Model A,” “Model B,” or “Grok 4.6”—sit at separate desks labeled Coding, Mathematics, Legal Reasoning, General Knowledge, and Real-World Knowledge Work. frontier-model: A clean editorial illustration shows a steep, glowing mountain ridge representing “frontier capability,” with a dashed, continuously moving boundary line tracing the leading edge upward and rightward across dated marker posts from 2025 to mid-2026. On the crest stand four prominent, brightly lit humanoid figures labeled GPT‑5.6 family, Claude Opus 5, Fable 5, and Grok 4.6, each wearing a badge for its lab—OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI—and facing forward toward an open, hazy horizon of harder future benchmarks. token: A single illustration split vertically by a glowing model icon in the center: on the left, an incoming prompt is shown as a stream of text being sliced into small colored blocks, each block labeled as a whole short word, a fragment of a longer word, or a punctuation mark, with a caption reading “input tokens” and a price tag of “$2 per million” under a pile of modest coins; on the right, the model emits a similar stream of one-piece-at-a-time blocks forming a reply, but these output token blocks are visibly larger and tagged “$6 per million,” with correspondingly bigger dollar signs or a taller stack of coins, visually conveying that tokens are the basic units read and written, and that output tokens cost more than input tokens.
